job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Ben Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thank you for talking with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I wake up around seven, make coffee and start at 8:30 at a fintech company in Toronto's financial district. I'm a junior software developer on the payments team, mostly writing and testing small services, with an AI coding assistant open all day. I did software engineering at the University of Waterloo and had one internship at a bank.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that I ship something small almost every week and see it used. What wears me out is the on-call rotation, because a payment bug at 3am is no fun. I share an apartment with my friend Kenji, and on weekends I tinker with a small budgeting app and read about index funds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's helpful and overrated at the same time. At work I'd keep using it, because it does save time, but I'd tell people it doesn't understand why a payment rule exists. The tool writes the code, but I'm still the one who gets the call at 3am when it breaks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm calm. My skills are in demand, my pay is good, I have no debt and about eight months saved. I might even benefit if it stays a plateau, since I'm already fast with the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going: learn the payment systems properly, take on an on-call rotation and put 500 dollars a month into an index fund. I'd keep building my budgeting app on weekends. Maybe in a year I'd ask for a bigger project.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's just a good day at the office, extended.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use AI tools every day. What does a normal hour look like with them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I describe what I want, the assistant writes a first version, and I read it, fix it and write tests. About half the code starts that way. If I don't understand a line, I don't ship it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Kenji, your flatmate, about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Kenji it's a better version of what we have already. He's a graphic designer and he's less relaxed. I'd say that he should try it, since it's easier to judge something you've used.

say: I'd say AI is **helpful and overrated** at once.
I'd tell people the tool doesn't know why a payment **rule** exists.
think: I'm **calm**, because my skills are in demand and I use the tools fast.
I have no debt and about **eight months** saved.
do: Learn the payment systems properly and take on an **on-call** rotation.
Put **500 dollars** a month into an index fund.
Keep building my **budgeting app** on weekends.
feel: **Calm**, like a good day at the office extended.
S0.quote: The tool writes the code, but I'm still the one who gets the call at 3am when it breaks.
fieldNote: He treats the assistant as a **junior pair** he reviews, and never ships code he doesn't understand.
Security comes from skills, savings and a short job market lag.
His flatmate Kenji, a designer, is more exposed.

steps.text: Take on an on-call rotation and learn the payment systems
Put 500 dollars a month into a broad index fund
Keep building the budgeting app on weekends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's big and the people who use it well will win. At work I'd volunteer to write our team's guide for using the assistant safely. Writing code is going to be the cheap part, and knowing what to build is going to be the expensive part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'm calm and a bit excited. Junior roles will shrink in general, and companies will want fewer people for the same output. But I already work this way, so I'd be one of the ones they keep, and I think I'd get more responsibility sooner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for more design and customer-facing tasks. I'd take a course on system design and risk, and use more of the tools on my own app. I'd keep saving and put a bit more into shares, since I think the companies that use this well will grow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly good. There's a bit of nerves, like before a race, and it's the useful kind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of your own work would the machine take next?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The easy tickets. Fix a typo, add a field, write a test. Within a year or two the assistant will do the lot, and I'll be reviewing instead of writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your team would feel it most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The newest juniors and the people who refuse the tools. I've seen a colleague who won't touch it, and he's slower every month. I like him, so I've offered to pair with him.

I'd volunteer to write a team guide for **safe** use.
think: I'm calm and a bit **excited**, since I already work this way.

do: Ask for more **design** and customer-facing tasks.
Take a course on **system design** and risk.

feel: **Good**, with a bit of nerves like before a race.
S1.quote: Writing code is going to be the cheap part, and knowing what to build is going to be the expensive part.
fieldNote: He expects to **win** from the change and admits others will lose.
He helps a resistant colleague rather than judging him.
He leans toward investing in firms that use AI well.

steps.text: Write the team's guide for using the coding assistant safely
Take an evening course on system design and risk
Put 700 dollars a month into the index fund and some shares

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's moving faster than anyone is ready for, and we need to be honest. At work I'd say my own role could be gone, and so could my manager's. The scariest part is that I know how to use it, and I still can't tell where I fit in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be anxious. Full AGI means the thinking work I do is done by something cheaper, and companies will cut juniors first and then everyone else. Robots take three more years, but I'm a keyboard person, so that doesn't help me much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build my savings fast, maybe 1,200 dollars a month, and turn the budgeting app into a real product. I'd start looking for work that needs a human, like running AI systems for small firms or sales for software. I'd also put some money into broad index funds, because if the economy grows, I want a share.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with a strong drive to do something. It's more like sprinting than freezing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years, what exactly would you do in the first month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the first month talking to ten people who run small firms, to see what they'd pay for. I'd also put my savings in a safe place and set a target for six months. It's only a plan, but I'm adaptable and I'd rather move early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your parents in Vancouver?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them I'm fine and I'm planning, and my mother would say I should come home. They have a house in Vancouver, so I could. I'd keep that as a back-up, not the first plan.

I'd be honest that my own role could be gone.
think: I'm **anxious**, since full AGI would do my thinking work more cheaply.
I'm a keyboard person, so the three extra **robot years** help me little.
do: Build savings fast, about **1,200 dollars** a month.

Put money into broad **index funds** to share in growth.
feel: **Anxious**, with a drive to act: more sprinting than freezing.
S2.quote: The scariest part is that I know how to use it, and I still can't tell where I fit in two years.
fieldNote: He treats fear as a **to-do list**, which fits his adaptive style.
The back-up plan is his parents' house, kept as second choice.
He sees growth as something he wants a share of.

steps.text: Talk to ten small firms about what they'd pay the budgeting app to do
Put spare money into broad index funds
Keep my parents' Vancouver house as a back-up plan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short, but it's enough to act, and I'd tell friends to start now. At work I'd push for a plan for juniors, like paid learning time. Five years is long enough to start a company and short enough that you can't waste any of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm uneasy more than scared. I think my current job won't look the same by 2031, and a lot of coding jobs will be gone. But I'm used to change, and I think my pay would hold if I move early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd get a promotion if I can, then start a small business on the side, building tools for local shops. I'd save 800 dollars a month and add to my index fund. By year three I'd decide whether the side project can replace my salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful and a bit nervous. I feel I can steer it, and that's a good feeling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the three extra years before robots reach hands-on work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not as a pure coder. I'd move towards building products, talking to customers and managing AI systems. That's still software, but with more people in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stay in software?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, since I'm not a hands-on person. But I'd learn how to manage robots in a warehouse or a shop, because someone will have to. That might be a nice business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to build something real, and I'd tell friends to learn a bit of everything. At work I'd keep learning and shipping. Ten years gives me time to build a business, buy a place and still change course twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm calm, I think. At 32 I could have my own company or a senior role guiding AI systems. If I stay adaptable and keep investing, I could be fine, though I know it's easy to say when you have savings and family backing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job, grow my side business and keep putting 600 dollars a month in funds. I'd buy a small apartment around 27 if prices allow. I'd use new tools as soon as they come out, and teach juniors what I learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and optimistic. A decade makes it feel like a normal career with extra turns.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be different if you knew it was ten years away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be less hurried. With two years I'd sprint, and with ten I'd build slowly. I'd also give back, maybe mentor students at Waterloo.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about buying a place?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I'd like to buy at around 27, with a partner if I have one. The date doesn't scare me off buying. A home is a home, and I'd rent out a room if I needed to.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. I use these tools all day and I'm still not sure where a junior developer fits in two years. What would help is a savings cushion, quick retraining money and honest talk from employers about what they plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I've been lucky, with a good school and family support. I'd like the tools to help people who don't have that. Otherwise the winners will win by default.

headlineQuote: I use these tools all day and I'm still not sure where a junior developer fits in two years.
portrait: Ben is **22**, a software engineering graduate working as a junior developer at a fintech company in Toronto.
He uses AI tools every day, has no debt and about eight months saved, and his parents in Vancouver would back him.
He is centre and pragmatic, **blames** nobody, and wants honest talk from employers and quick retraining money.
He is adaptive: he moves early, builds a **side business** and invests, and admits his calm rests on luck.
biggestWorry: AI by **2028** worries him most, because two years leaves no clear place for a junior developer.
whatWouldHelp: A **savings cushion**, quick retraining money and honest plans from employers.
